pr_body:
On some conditions (particularly when mobile CPUs are going to sleep),
the posix_fallocate(), which is called when a new journal file is allocated,
can return -1 (EINTR). This is counted as a fatal error. So the journald
closes both old and journals, and simply throwing away further incoming
events, because of no log files open.

Let's restart posix_fallocate() in a case of EINTR.

Fixes: #19041

Signed-off-by: Igor Zhbanov <i.zhbanov@omprussia.ru>
pr_comments: ptrace attach/detach might cause EINTR iirc, since they cannot attach while the process is in kernel mode, so it synthesizes EINTR, so that it can attach afterwards
I've run entire systemd-journald from the start under strace. And 600 megabytes after start, I've got the error. So it shouldn't be related to attaching/detaching.

I don't think there's any POSIX requirement in general for `EINTR` to actually be accompanied by a signal, so it's been getting abused (or maybe that's a "feature"?)

In terms of process freezing/thawing I can imagine why the kernel would synthesize `EINTR` thawing blocking "slow" syscalls; it's assuming the caller may handle this explicitly and do something appropriate upon noticing potentially a lot of real-time has passed, or it'll just blindly restart the operation.

I'm short on time currently, but wonder if instead of performing a potentially infinite retry loop here, why isn't journald ever re-attempting the journal open after this one error is realized?  That seems like it could be considered a bug, for journald to never resume logging after what could be just a transient condition causing journal open failures.

> I'm short on time currently, but wonder if instead of performing a potentially infinite retry loop here, why isn't journald ever re-attempting the journal open after this one error is realized? That seems like it could be considered a bug, for journald to never resume logging after what could be just a transient condition causing journal open failures.

Well, that's what I'm exactly written in the issue. :-) So, yes, my current fix is more about the particular issue. But surely jourlnald should be more resilient to transient errors like no disk space, etc. And should try at least to make some number of attempts with may be some delay.

> > I'm short on time currently, but wonder if instead of performing a potentially infinite retry loop here, why isn't journald ever re-attempting the journal open after this one error is realized? That seems like it could be considered a bug, for journald to never resume logging after what could be just a transient condition causing journal open failures.
> 
> Well, that's what I'm exactly written in the issue. :-) So, yes, my current fix is more about the particular issue. But surely jourlnald should be more resilient to transient errors like no disk space, etc. And should try at least to make some number of attempts with may be some delay.

Perhaps if the higher-order issue of journald recovery from errors is addressed, this specific call site's error handling becomes irrelevant?

Either way, `TEMP_FAILURE_RETRY()` is arguably an unbounded busy loop spinning on a syscall.  At a glance, my knee-jerk reaction is to NAK its use here or anywhere in the systemd source.

If retrying at the call site is appropriate, make it both bounded, and perhaps with an increasing delay until giving up.  I don't recall if there's already a helper for doing that in-tree.  Logging the >1 retries might also be desirable.

In the scenario we're specifically thinking about here, we expect the normal execution to be just a single retry after an EINTR, correct?
Added retry count. So now it will call posix_fallocate() at most 2 times.

As for generic journald improvements, I don't know current architecture guidelines, i.e. how to name retry attempts option? Should it be made separate for volatile and persistent storages?
The same is for the retry delay. Should it be fixed, or doubled after each attempt until some maximal duration reached?
At what journald function nesting level should we try to restart?
Or should we just abort the journald entirely so systemd can simply restart it? (Although we can lose some messages.)

So this task is not complex, but requires to know current best systemd's architectural practices.

issue_context.title: On some errors journald can close the journal and not try to open the new ones
issue_context.body:
I've found a strange bug that systemd-journald stopped to write new messages on disk, while leaving the journal files in the corrupted state.
By running it under strace I've found at least one cause of it: sometimes fallocate() (which is called during journal rotation) can return -1 (EINTR). (I don't know yet why this could happen.)
Then the journald prints the error in the dmesg: "Failed to create new runtime journal: Interrupted system call" then simply accepting further incoming events and not writing it anywhere, because no journal files are open.

You can test it with strace fault injection:
`strace -v -s 8192 -y -f -e inject=fallocate:error=EINTR:when=5+3 /usr/lib/systemd/systemd-journald`
Then you can send -SIGUSR2 a couple of times to force the journal rotation.
Then you can check in the `/proc/PID/fd` that no journal files are open.

So I can see 2 issues here:
1) It would be better to handle EINTR or to set-up automatic syscall restarts with the sigaction().
2) Journald could do better when it is unable to create the new journal file. I.e. it could at least try to make it again after some time.
comments:
I suggest:
1) Use automatic syscalls restart (SA_RESTART flag for sigaction())
2) The journal should make several attampts (configurable option) with some delay (configurable option) after that it should terminate, so the systemd can restart it.
Should we wait for a fix, or are you expecting us to propose it?
